title: Mac not detecting external monitor fix: what to try first on Apple silicon and Intel
metaTitle: Mac not detecting external monitor fix: free steps that work
description: Mac not detecting an external monitor? Hold Option, open Displays, click Detect Displays. Then check the cable, hub, and adapter. Free fixes from Apple's guide.
targetKeyword: mac not detecting external monitor fix
secondaryKeywords: usb-c adapter mac monitor not working
intro: If your Mac doesn't detect an external monitor, start with Apple's own fix. Hold Option, open System Settings > Displays, and click Detect Displays. If the screen stays dark, unplug the display, skip any hub or dock, and plug it straight into a port on the Mac.
tldr: Hold Option, open System Settings > Displays, and click Detect Displays. Apple lists this first, and it costs nothing.
Reseat the cable at both ends, then plug the display straight into a Mac port. Hubs and docks cause many dark screens.
On Apple silicon, watch for the accessory prompt. If you declined it, the display stays dark until you allow it.
Check your Mac model's external display limit against your resolution and refresh rate before you blame the cable.
If the monitor stays dark after a restart and a cable swap, suspect hardware. Contact Apple or the monitor maker.

blocks.text: Detect Displays on Mac: Apple's first fix

Apple's own guide, HT201177, starts with one step. Hold the Option key and open System Settings > Displays. While you hold Option, Detect Displays replaces Night Shift. Click it, then wait a few seconds. This asks the Mac to search for displays again, so start here.
If nothing changes, move to the physical checks. Work through them in this order. The cheapest checks come first, and each one narrows the fault.

items: Hold Option, open System Settings > Displays, and click Detect Displays.
Unplug the display at both ends. Wait a few seconds, then plug it back in firmly.
Remove any hub or dock. Plug the display straight into a port on the Mac.
Restart the Mac. If it's frozen, hold the power button about 10 seconds.

blocks.text: The order matters for a reason. Detect Displays costs nothing. Reseating a cable takes a minute. Removing a hub gives the clearest test, because it takes the middle out of the chain.
Why a Mac stops seeing an external monitor

Most dark external screens trace back to four places. The cable or adapter, a hub in the middle, a limit on how many displays the Mac can drive, or a prompt you didn't answer. Each one needs a different test. Sorting the symptom first saves time.

A cable that charges is not the same as a cable that carries video. Apple requires any USB-C or Thunderbolt adapter for a display to be compliant with DisplayPort Alt Mode, Thunderbolt 3, or Thunderbolt 4. A charging cable from a drawer of spares can look right and show nothing.

items: Dark from the first plug-in: suspect the cable, adapter, or port.
Worked before a hub or dock was added: suspect the hub.
Failed after you added a second or third screen: suspect the display limit.
Failed on Apple silicon after a dock swap: suspect the accessory prompt.
Works on another laptop: suspect your Mac's settings, port, or macOS state.
Works on no computer at all: suspect the monitor or its cable.

blocks.text: A worked example: a dark monitor after a dock swap

Say you run a MacBook Pro through a USB-C dock to a monitor. You unplug the laptop for a meeting, then plug it back in. The keyboard works, but the monitor stays black. Here is how to sort that out in a few minutes.

First, hold Option and click Detect Displays. Nothing changes. Second, remove the dock and plug the monitor straight into a Mac port, using an adapter you know works. The screen wakes up. The fault sits in the dock path, not in the monitor.

Notice what you did. You changed one part at a time, and you kept the monitor the same. If you had swapped the cable, the dock, and the adapter at once, you couldn't tell which change fixed it. Keep the dock out of the chain until you test it alone.
What a dark display costs a developer

A dark screen costs more than the minutes you spend fixing it. You lose the window layout, the thread of your work, and sometimes a build you were watching. Few public sources measure display faults on their own. The best numbers cover tool problems in general.

Lokalise surveyed 500 American developers. It found they lose an average of 3 hours per week to tool failures, outages, and workflow problems, close to 20 workdays per year. The survey comes from a localization vendor, and its fieldwork dates and sampling aren't stated. Treat it as a rough signal, not a measurement.

To turn hours into money, use the Bureau of Labor Statistics wage for software developers. The May 2025 median was $135,980 a year. Divide by 2,080 hours and you get about $65 per hour in base pay, before benefits or overhead. Three hours at that rate is about $195 a week.

blocks.text: Those figures describe tool trouble in general, not monitors. Use them to decide how much time a dark display deserves. Your own hourly rate is the number that matters most.
Apple silicon adds an accessory prompt you can miss

On Macs with Apple silicon, macOS may ask you to allow the accessory to connect. The accessory is your display. If you decline, the display stays dark. The prompt can sit behind another window, or appear while you type in another app.

If you declined and can't find the prompt, unplug the display and wait a few seconds. Reconnect it, then watch the screen before you touch anything else. Allow the connection when the prompt shows for the display you expect.
Display limits by model, resolution, and refresh rate

Every Mac can drive only so many external displays at once. The limit depends on the Mac model, plus the resolution and refresh rate of each screen. Apple says a display stays dark if it goes past the maximum. A resolution or refresh rate above the supported limit can also cause dim output.

Apple's support page doesn't list the counts. It links to per-model pages instead. Third-party counts differ from each other, so read the figure on Apple's technical specifications for your exact model. Then test with fewer screens or a lower resolution.
USB-C adapters, hubs, and docks

Adapters are the weakest link for many people. A USB-C to HDMI dongle, a cheap multiport hub, or an old dock can carry power and data while the video path fails. Test with the display in a Mac port first. Bring the hub back only after the direct test works.

When you buy a replacement, look for DisplayPort Alt Mode, Thunderbolt 3, or Thunderbolt 4 compliance. Apple says to check with the manufacturer for compatibility with your Mac and display model. A product label alone doesn't prove it works with your setup.
Third-party tools for display settings

Lunar and BetterDisplay are the two tools people reach for. Both work after macOS sees the display. Lunar says its main feature is DDC brightness control of the real monitor. BetterDisplay describes virtual screens, HiDPI scaling, and brightness, volume, and color control. Neither is a detection fix.

Lunar sells Lunar Pro as a one-time $23 lifetime license, with a 14-day trial. Its free tier caps Manual Mode at 100 adjustments per day. BetterDisplay's page showed no price in our check, so look at its official site. That page also warns about lookalike download sites.
Mistakes that waste the most time

items: Retesting the same bad cable. Swap in one you know carries video.
Changing three things at once. You can't tell which change worked.
Declining the accessory prompt by reflex, then waiting for the screen to wake.
Blaming the monitor before testing it on another computer.
Testing through the hub only, and never in a Mac port.
Installing a display app and expecting it to find a dark monitor.
Skipping the firmware check for a non-Apple monitor.

blocks.text: When the external display still won't show

If the steps above fail, a hardware fault is possible. A June 2025 Apple Community thread describes a MacBook Pro M2 Max (2023) that stopped showing output over HDMI to an LG 27ML600 after about a year of use. The owner tried power cycling, Safe Mode, a new user account, and deleting EDID cache files. Resolution changes, other HDMI cables, and the monitor's other input failed too. The thread closed without a confirmed fix.

That thread is one case, not a count. It doesn't tell you how common the fault is. It does show what to bring to Apple or the monitor maker. List every test you ran, the result of each, your Mac model, and your monitor model.
Where Lazur helps with a dark monitor

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where Detect Displays is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do the steps, and it guides you one click at a time.

Lazur does not click buttons for you. It doesn't change settings, fix a cable, or tell you whether a port is dead. Use it to find the right control, follow the steps, and dictate notes. If you want it on your Mac, you can [download Lazur here](/download).

If the work involves client or patient data, follow your employer's rules. That applies to screenshots and voice requests. Lazur sends audio and the screenshot to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Check your employer's policy first.
Keep the checklist handy and stop early

Use the plan below as a checklist. Stop at the first step that wakes the screen. Write down what worked, so the next dark screen takes less time. If your Bluetooth audio drops too, read [why Bluetooth headphones keep disconnecting from Mac](/for/developers/problems/bluetooth-headphones-keep-disconnecting-mac).

faq.question: Why won't my Mac detect my external monitor?
faq.answer: The usual causes are a cable or adapter that doesn't carry video, a hub or dock in the path, a declined accessory prompt on Apple silicon, or a display set past the Mac's limit. Start with Detect Displays in System Settings > Displays. Then remove the hub and plug straight into the Mac.

faq.question: How do I find Detect Displays on a Mac?
faq.answer: Open System Settings > Displays, then hold the Option key. Detect Displays replaces Night Shift while you hold it. Click it and wait a few seconds. Apple's guide is HT201177 on support.apple.com.

faq.question: Does any USB-C cable work for an external monitor?
faq.answer: No. The adapter must be compliant with DisplayPort Alt Mode, Thunderbolt 3, or Thunderbolt 4. Apple says to check with the manufacturer for your Mac and display model. A charging-only cable won't show video.

faq.question: What if my monitor works on another laptop?
faq.answer: Then the monitor is probably fine, and the fault sits on your Mac side or in the path. Check the adapter, the port, the display limit, and any pending macOS update. If it fails everywhere, suspect the monitor or the cable.

faq.question: How many external monitors can a Mac drive?
faq.answer: It depends on the Mac model, plus the resolution and refresh rate of each screen. Apple's support page links to per-model pages rather than listing counts. Read the figure for your exact model on Apple's technical specifications.

faq.question: Will Lunar or BetterDisplay make a dark monitor show up?
faq.answer: Usually not. Both apps work after macOS sees the display. Lunar sells a one-time $23 lifetime license with a 14-day trial. BetterDisplay's price wasn't clear in our check, so use its official site.

faq.question: Can Lazur fix the connection for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur doesn't click buttons, change settings, or repair cables. It can point at Detect Displays, guide you one click at a time, explain messages, and dictate notes.

faq.question: When should I stop and contact Apple?
faq.answer: Stop when the display stays dark after a restart, a direct port connection, a known good cable, and a firmware check. Bring your Mac model, your monitor model, and a list of tests. Apple or the monitor maker can test the hardware.

costs.title: Lost work time
costs.text: A dark monitor costs time before it costs anything else. You stop coding, reopen windows, and hunt for settings. Public data is thin for this exact fault. The closest number comes from a vendor survey of 500 American developers. They reported about 3 hours per week lost to tool failures in general, so your monitor share is a part of that total.

costs.title: Your base pay per hour
costs.text: The Bureau of Labor Statistics put the May 2025 median for software developers at $135,980 a year. Divide by 2,080 hours and you get about $65 per hour. That is base pay only, before benefits or overhead. A stalled hour costs that much in wages, even when you're only waiting for a screen.

costs.title: Broken focus after a dark screen
costs.text: A monitor that drops mid-task pulls your windows onto the laptop screen. You rebuild the layout, then rebuild your train of thought. No source we checked measures this for display faults. Treat it as real but unmeasured. A separate guide covers the recovery: [recovering focus after interruptions](/for/developers/problems/developer-context-switching-recovery-time).

costs.title: Hardware and replacement parts
costs.text: If the display is dead, you may need a new adapter, cable, or monitor. This page doesn't list parts prices, because we did not verify them. Test each part before you buy. Check the adapter maker's compatibility page and the monitor maker's support page first.

costs.title: Screens with client or patient data
costs.text: If the dark screen holds client, patient, or other regulated data, follow your employer's rules. That applies before you share screenshots, logs, or voice requests with anyone, including AI tools. Ask your IT team what they allow before you ask for help online.

causes.title: The cable or adapter does not carry video
causes.text: Many USB-C cables charge a Mac but don't carry video. A display path needs an adapter compliant with DisplayPort Alt Mode, Thunderbolt 3, or Thunderbolt 4. Apple says to check with the manufacturer for your Mac and display model. Cheap dongles and charging-only cables are the usual suspects.

causes.title: A hub or dock sits in the middle
causes.text: Apple's guide says to plug the display directly into a Mac port if it runs through a hub or dock. A dock can power a keyboard and mouse while its video path fails. Many people test with the hub still in place, which makes a dead display look like a dead monitor.

causes.title: The Mac hits its external display limit
causes.text: Each Mac can drive a set number of external displays. The number depends on the model, plus the resolution and refresh rate of each display. Apple says a display stays dark if it goes past the maximum. Adding one more screen to a working setup can be the whole problem.

causes.title: The accessory prompt was declined
causes.text: On Apple silicon, macOS may ask you to allow the accessory, which is your display, to connect. Decline it, and the display stays dark. The prompt is easy to miss when it appears behind other windows or during a dock swap.

causes.title: Closed lid, sleep, or a loose connection
causes.text: According to Apple, a closed-lid laptop needs power plus an external keyboard and mouse. A loose plug can look like a dead display. Apple's steps ask you to confirm the cable sits firmly in the correct port. Check the port and the plug before you blame the monitor.

causes.title: Out-of-date firmware on the monitor
causes.text: macOS updates deliver firmware for Apple displays. For other brands, Apple says to get the latest firmware from the manufacturer. Old firmware is a possible cause, though no source we checked ranks it. Check the maker's support page, and follow its update steps exactly.

causes.title: A hardware fault in the port or display
causes.text: Sometimes the problem is physical. A June 2025 Apple Community thread about a MacBook Pro M2 Max (2023) describes an HDMI output that stopped working after about a year. Power cycling, Safe Mode, and cable swaps did not fix it. A fault like that calls for Apple or the monitor maker.

fixes.title: Detect Displays with the Option key
fixes.text: Hold Option (⌥), then open System Settings > Displays. While you hold Option, Detect Displays replaces Night Shift. Click it and give the Mac a few seconds to search. This is Apple's first step, and it costs nothing. Don't skip it because the cable feels like the problem.

fixes.title: Unplug, reconnect, and seat the cable
fixes.text: Unplug the display from both ends. Wait a few seconds. Plug it back in, and push the connector until it seats fully. Apple says to confirm the cable is firmly in the correct port. A half-seated connector looks exactly like a dead monitor, so check it twice.

fixes.title: Plug straight into a Mac port
fixes.text: Remove any hub or dock. Plug the display into a port on the Mac itself. If the screen wakes up, the hub or dock is the problem. Test a different hub later, and don't rely on the one that failed.

fixes.title: Swap one part at a time
fixes.text: Change one thing per test. Try a cable you know carries video. Then try the adapter. Keep the monitor and the Mac the same throughout. Write down each result, so you can see which change actually worked.

fixes.title: Restart, or force a restart
fixes.text: Apple suggests a restart. Choose Apple menu > Restart. If the Mac is frozen and the menu won't respond, hold the power button about 10 seconds, then press it again to start. Restart after each cable change, not only at the end.

fixes.title: Approve the accessory prompt
fixes.text: On Apple silicon, watch for the prompt that asks you to allow the accessory to connect. Allow it for the display you expect. If you declined and can't find the prompt, unplug the display, wait a few seconds, and reconnect. Then watch the screen again.

fixes.title: Update macOS and monitor firmware
fixes.text: Open Apple menu > System Settings > General > Software Update and install pending updates. macOS updates can include firmware for Apple displays. For another brand, check the manufacturer's support page for firmware, and follow its steps exactly.

fixes.title: Check the display limit and resolution
fixes.text: Look up your Mac model on Apple's technical specifications and note its external display limit. Then open System Settings > Displays and try a lower resolution or refresh rate. Apple warns that settings above supported limits can cause dim output.

fixes.title: Test with a new user account
fixes.text: The Apple Community thread tried Safe Mode and a new user account, and neither fixed that display. You can run similar tests to separate software from hardware. If the display works in a new user account, your profile or its settings may be the cause. If it fails everywhere, suspect hardware.

fixes.title: Skip third-party apps until the display shows
fixes.text: Lunar and BetterDisplay control or enhance a display once macOS sees it. Neither is a detection fix. Wait until the display appears in System Settings > Displays before you install one. Download only from official sites, since lookalike sites exist.

plan.label: Now
plan.title: Run Detect Displays
plan.text: Hold Option, open System Settings > Displays, and click Detect Displays. Give it a few seconds. If the screen wakes, you're done. If not, move to the next step.

plan.label: Next
plan.title: Reseat the cable
plan.text: Unplug the display at both ends. Wait a few seconds, then plug it back in firmly into the same port. Remove any hub or dock while you test.

plan.label: Then
plan.title: Test one part at a time
plan.text: Plug the display straight into a Mac port. Swap the cable, then the adapter, changing one part per test. Write down the combination that works.

plan.label: After
plan.title: Sleep, wake, restart
plan.text: Sleep and wake the Mac, then restart it. If the Mac is frozen, hold the power button about 10 seconds. On Apple silicon, watch for the accessory prompt and allow it.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Check updates and limits
plan.text: Open Apple menu > System Settings > General > Software Update. For a non-Apple monitor, check the maker's support page for firmware. Confirm your model's display limit on Apple's technical specifications.

plan.label: If still dark
plan.title: Stop and escalate
plan.text: If the display fails after a restart, a direct port, a known good cable, and a firmware check, suspect hardware. Contact Apple or the monitor maker with your test notes.
